Reactivity: Svelte's reactivity is compiler-driven: assignments to variables automatically trigger DOM updates without a virtual DOM or manual state management. The compiler instruments variable assignments to invalidate dependencies.
Templates: Svelte templates extend HTML with {expression} bindings, {#if} blocks, {#each} loops, and {#await} for promises. The template syntax is concise and compiles to highly optimized imperative DOM operations.
Logic: Svelte provides logic blocks ({#if}, {:else if}, {:else}) and loops ({#each}, {:else}) within templates. Loops support destructuring and index tracking without special directives.

Svelte Data.exp: Working with data and APIs in Svelte.

Vitest: Vitest integrates seamlessly with SvelteKit projects for fast unit and integration testing with Vite-powered HMR, Jest-compatible API, and native ESM support.
Playwright: Playwright is the recommended E2E testing framework for SvelteKit, providing cross-browser automation, network interception, and component testing across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.

Props: Props in Svelte are declared with the export keyword inside a component script, allowing parent components to pass data. Props can have default values and are reactive when reassigned.
Slots: Slots allow parent components to inject content into a child's layout. Named slots and slot props enable flexible component composition and scoped content distribution.
Events: Svelte uses the createEventDispatcher helper to forward custom events from child to parent components. DOM events are bound directly with on: directives like on:click.

Writable: Writable stores are the most basic store type, providing set, update, and subscribe methods. They allow cross-component state sharing without prop drilling and auto-subscribe in Svelte templates.

import { writable } from 'svelte/store';
export const count = writable(0);
Derived: Derived stores compute values from one or more dependent stores, updating automatically when their sources change. They support transformations and can produce derived writable stores.
Custom Stores: Custom stores encapsulate logic by wrapping the store primitives and exposing a controlled API. They hide implementation details while providing the same subscribe contract for template binding.

onMount: onMount is the most commonly used lifecycle function, executing after the component is first rendered. It's ideal for data fetching, DOM measurements, and cleanup via returned teardown functions.
beforeUpdate: beforeUpdate runs before the DOM is updated after state changes, making it useful for reading the DOM before Svelte patches it. It's the counterpart to afterUpdate.
afterUpdate: afterUpdate runs after the DOM has been updated following state changes, suitable for DOM measurements or scrolling to newly rendered elements. It fires after every component update.
onDestroy: onDestroy registers a callback that runs when a component is unmounted, making it the right place for cleanup like clearing timers, unsubscribing from stores, or canceling network requests.

Tweened: Tweened stores smoothly interpolate numeric values over time, creating animated transitions between states. They support configurable easing functions and interpolation durations.
const progress = tweened(0, { duration: 400, easing: cubicOut });
Spring: Spring stores simulate physics-based animations using stiffness, damping, and mass parameters. They create natural-feeling motion that responds dynamically to changing target values.
Transitions: Svelte's built-in transitions (fade, slide, scale, fly) and custom transition functions provide declarative enter/exit animations. They work with the transition: directive and support in/out modifiers.
Animations: Svelte's animate: directive enables FLIP-based animations for list reordering, automatically calculating position changes and animating elements to their new positions smoothly.

Actions: Actions are Svelte's approach to integrating with DOM elements imperatively, similar to use:action. They receive the element and optional parameters, returning lifecycle methods like destroy for cleanup.
Context API: The context API allows passing data to a component and all its descendants without prop drilling. setContext and getContext are scoped to the component tree, not globally like stores.
Special Elements: Svelte provides special elements like <svelte:body>, <svelte:head>, <svelte:window>, and <svelte:options> for declaring side effects and configuration directly in templates.

Routing: SvelteKit uses filesystem-based routing where each +page.svelte file in src/routes creates a route. Dynamic parameters are captured with [bracket] notation in directory names.
Endpoints: Endpoints are server-only API routes defined as +server.js files exporting request handlers. They handle GET, POST, PUT, DELETE requests and return JSON or other responses.
SSR: SvelteKit renders pages server-side by default, generating HTML on the server for fast initial loads and SEO. SSR can be disabled per route or globally for fully client-rendered apps.

Runes: $state, $derived, $effect: Svelte 5 introduces runes — explicit reactive primitives that replace the Svelte 4 let / export let / $: magic. $state() creates reactive state. $derived() creates derived values that update automatically. $effect() runs side effects when tracked dependencies change. $props() explicitly declares component props. Runes work both in .svelte files and .svelte.js/.svelte.ts modules, enabling shared reactive logic outside components. $bindable() creates two-way bindable props. Runes make reactivity explicit and TypeScript-friendly.

Svelte 5 Snippets & Event Handling: Svelte 5 introduces snippets ({#snippet}) for reusable template fragments, replacing slots in many cases. Event handlers use callbacks (onclick={handler}) instead of on:click. Event modifiers are attached with function calls. Cross-component state uses runes in .svelte.ts files. onMount/onDestroy lifecycle functions are now imported. bind:value works with $bindable() for two-way bindings. class and style attributes support objects and arrays.

Snippet Blocks: Snippets are reusable template fragments defined with {#snippet name} and rendered with {@render name}. They accept parameters and can be passed between components as first-class template values.
Snippet Props: Snippets passed as props allow parent components to inject template content into children, replacing slot-based composition with a more explicit and type-safe pattern.
Children Snippet: The implicit children snippet captures default content between component tags. It provides a cleaner alternative to the default slot for wrapping content in layout components.
